6.text: Only the names of the principal villages are here given, because the

7.text: smaller ones mentioned by many travellers are not fixed dwelling-places. They

8.text: are simply hunting-stations, that are used for a few years, and afterwards aban-

9.text: doned for other places a few miles away. The name belongs to the locality,

10.text: not to the village. Even the larger villages are not very stable; and the

11.text: population often desert one and move to another, according to the changing

12.text: conditions of seal-hunting. However, those among the smaller settlements

13.text: which were mentioned by several older travellers, and which happen to be

14.text: inhabited at the present time, are included in the following list.

16.text: The villages on the Pacific coast are as follows: —

17.text: Veᵋñ, in Anadyr Bay, near the mouth of the Anadyr River.² The Russians subsequently founded

18.text: a settlement near by, and called it Mariinsky Post. In former times the Chukchee village lay

19.text: nearer the open sea, on the low sandy shore of Geëk Land. Veᵋñ has at present 7 native

21.text: Mɪˊs˙qᴀn (“hill”), on the west point of the long, narrow island Mɪˊs˙qᴀn, ³ in Holy Cross Bay; and

22.text: Rêˊtkên (“clayish”), on the east point of the same island. During my visit in 1901 the former

23.text: village had 3 houses, and, besides, 1 family was living a few miles off; while in two places

24.text: there were 6 tents of some very poor half Maritime, half Reindeer people. The total population

25.text: was 41 (according to the Register, 7 houses, 30 inhabitants). Rêˊtkên had 6 houses with 35

27.text: Farther along the shore, on Cape Wuˊkwên (“stony”), there used to be a small settlement whose

28.text: inhabitants afterwards turned to reindeer-breeding and went inland.

29.text: ¹ In his statistics, Krause gives for the large village Uñiˊsak (Indian Point) only 13 houses “from personal

30.text: observation.” He evidently confounds the small village Kuˊkun with the larger Luˊᵋren, since he states that there

31.text: are 20 houses in Kuˊkun, and only 2 in Luˊᵋren, whereas in reality the numbers are the reverse.

32.text: ² On the Middle Anadyr live about ten Chukchee families scattered in five or six places. Of these,

33.text: Chikayeva has two families, and Under-the-Cliffs three. The first name has been borrowed by the Chukchee

34.text: from the Russianized natives; the second name has the same meaning, both in the Chukchee and in the Russian

35.text: languages. The other settlements are unstable.

36.text: ³ Long, narrow islands or spits, consisting of sand cast up by the waves, are met with everywhere on

37.text: the shores of Bering Sea and the Arctic Ocean, especially at the mouths of rivers or of narrow, deeply indented

38.text: bays. These islands are called by the Chukchee Teˊpän in the Pacific dialect, and Teˊpqän in the Arctic dialect. With

39.text: the Kamchadal and Koryak, where salmon is abundant, the villages near such spits lie on the mainland shore,

40.text: which is less exposed to the wind. Mouths of rivers and entrances to bays are very convenient places for

41.text: catching salmon, which enter there in masses for the purpose of spawning. The Maritime Chukchee and the

42.text: Eskimo, on the contrary, build their villages on the outward shore of such islands or spits for convenience of

43.text: sealing. The same is true of all islands lying near the shore. For instance, the Koryak village in Karagha

44.text: Bay, of northern Kamchatka, lies on the mainland shore, opposite the large island Karagha. The Chukchee

45.text: village in Kuluˊči Bay, on the contrary, is situated on the small island some distance away from the narrow

46.text: mouth of the bay. On Kihiˊni Island the village Kihiˊni lies on its outward northwestern shore. The villages

47.text: of Mɪˊs˙qᴀn, Rêˊtkên, and Yanřaˊkê-not are situated on sandy spits which lie at the entrance to the bays.
